qa_pairs.question: What is PathoIntern?
qa_pairs.answer: PathoIntern is a non-diagnostic AI triage assistant for blood smear pathology. It acts as a digital intern — performing first-pass analysis of blood smear patch images, flagging morphological anomalies, and displaying the most anomalous cases at the top of a prioritized worklist. The final clinical interpretation always remains with the licensed pathologist.

qa_pairs.question: Why was PathoIntern created?
qa_pairs.answer: PathoIntern was created to address the growing problem of pathologist workload and burnout. Blood smear review is one of the most cognitively demanding tasks in clinical pathology, and slide volumes are rising 5-10% annually without proportional growth in pathologist capacity. When critical slides are mixed with routine cases, urgent findings can be delayed by hours. PathoIntern ensures that pathologist expertise is always applied first to the cases that need it most.

qa_pairs.question: What is the vision of PathoIntern?
qa_pairs.answer: The vision is simple: No critical blood smear should wait for review. PathoIntern exists to close the gap between rising slide volumes and limited pathologist capacity — not by replacing pathologist expertise, but by ensuring that expertise is always applied first to the cases that need it most.

qa_pairs.question: What is the mission of PathoIntern?
qa_pairs.answer: The mission is to help pathologists prioritize blood smear slides through safe, non-diagnostic AI triage — so expertise is applied where it matters most. PathoIntern is designed to act as a digital intern — one that never sleeps, never fatigues, and never makes a final call.

qa_pairs.question: Is PathoIntern a diagnostic tool?
qa_pairs.answer: No. PathoIntern is explicitly non-diagnostic. It never assigns, suggests, or implies a clinical diagnosis. All output represents pattern similarity to previously reviewed cases and anomaly distance from a normal baseline — for triage prioritization only. The pathologist retains complete authority over every clinical decision. This is an architectural constraint enforced at every layer of the system, not a limitation.

qa_pairs.question: What does non-diagnostic mean in the context of PathoIntern?
qa_pairs.answer: Non-diagnostic means that PathoIntern never provides clinical diagnoses, diagnostic probabilities, or medical advice. Its scores represent how much a blood smear patch deviates from a normal baseline and how similar it is to previously seen cases. These are pattern-based triage signals, not diagnostic conclusions. Banned terms in the system include: diagnosis, diagnostic probability, likely, prediction, classify, and classification.

qa_pairs.question: What is a digital intern in pathology?
qa_pairs.answer: A digital intern is an AI assistant that performs the same first-pass review that a human pathology intern would — looking at slides, flagging anything that appears unusual, and suggesting which cases the senior pathologist should review first. Like a real intern, PathoIntern never makes final clinical decisions. It surfaces patterns and anomalies for expert review.

qa_pairs.question: What are the four mission pillars of PathoIntern?
qa_pairs.answer: The four mission pillars are: (1) First-Pass Analysis — CTransPath encodes each blood smear patch into a 768-dimensional feature vector for quantitative prioritization. (2) Priority by Anomaly Risk — k-NN anomaly detection scores each patch against a normal-cell baseline and maps it to a 0-100 criticality score across four tiers. (3) Incremental Learning — Pathologist verdicts (agree/disagree/modify) feed future model improvement cycles. (4) Transparent and Auditable — Every action is recorded in an immutable audit log with no unsupervised AI decisions.

qa_pairs.question: What are the explicit non-goals of PathoIntern?
qa_pairs.answer: PathoIntern has four explicit non-goals enforced as architectural constraints: (1) No Automated Diagnosis — output is triage priority only. (2) No CBC Data — the system operates on digitized image patches only, no lab values or clinical history. (3) No Unsupervised Decisions — every scored patch requires pathologist review. (4) No Diagnostic Probability — scores are pattern similarity, never probability of disease.

qa_pairs.question: What problem does PathoIntern solve?
qa_pairs.answer: PathoIntern solves the problem of unstructured blood smear review queues. Currently, pathologists review slides in the order they arrive (first-in-first-out), meaning a critical case with blast cells or hemoparasites can sit behind dozens of routine normal slides. PathoIntern analyzes each patch, scores it by anomaly risk, and reorders the worklist so the most critical cases surface first — reducing time-to-review for urgent findings.

qa_pairs.question: What research papers support PathoIntern?
qa_pairs.answer: PathoIntern is grounded in four peer-reviewed publications: (1) Khatab et al. (2024) in Critical Reviews in Clinical Laboratory Sciences — establishes pathologist workload and burnout as the core problem. (2) Baltruschat et al. (2021) in European Radiology — proves AI worklist prioritization reduces critical-case turnaround by 56%. (3) Dippel et al. (2024) in NEJM AI — validates CTransPath embeddings plus anomaly detection for clinical-grade triage. (4) Chen et al. (2024) in Nature Medicine — provides scientific validation for foundation model embeddings in computational pathology.

qa_pairs.question: What is the workload and burnout problem in pathology?
qa_pairs.answer: According to Khatab et al. (2024), pathologist workloads are increasing by approximately 5-10% annually across most departments, yet no standardized tool exists to measure or fairly distribute that workload. Burnout is driven by productivity demands, lack of recognition, and electronic health record burdens. The paper demonstrates that pathologists lack time-limiting factors for case sign-outs, making them uniquely vulnerable to fatigue-related performance degradation, which directly leads to diagnostic errors.

qa_pairs.question: How does AI worklist prioritization work?
qa_pairs.answer: Baltruschat et al. (2021) demonstrated that AI-driven worklist prioritization can reduce turnaround time for critical findings from 80.1 minutes to 35.6 minutes — a 56% reduction. The key insight is that the AI never renders diagnoses — it only reorders the queue by urgency so clinicians see critical cases first. The AI triages; the physician diagnoses. PathoIntern applies this same paradigm to blood smear pathology.

qa_pairs.question: What is the NEJM AI study about CTransPath?
qa_pairs.answer: Dippel et al. (2024) published in NEJM AI used CTransPath foundation model embeddings on 17 million histological images from 5,423 biopsy cases. The system was trained only on normal cases and used anomaly detection to flag rare conditions — achieving 95% AUROC for detecting anomalous pathologies. This is the closest methodological analog to PathoIntern: both use CTransPath 768-dim embeddings, both perform anomaly detection against a normal baseline, and both are designed to flag and prioritize cases for pathologist review.

qa_pairs.question: What is the UNI foundation model?
qa_pairs.answer: UNI is a self-supervised vision transformer developed by Mahmood Lab and published in Nature Medicine (Chen et al., 2024). It was pretrained on over 100 million histopathology images from more than 100,000 diagnostic whole-slide images spanning 20 major tissue types. UNI produces 4096-dimensional embeddings and significantly outperforms CTransPath. PathoIntern plans to upgrade from CTransPath (768-dim) to UNI (4096-dim) in Phase 2.

qa_pairs.question: How do these research papers connect?
qa_pairs.answer: The four papers form a cohesive argument chain: Paper 1 (Khatab) establishes the problem — pathologist workloads cause burnout and diagnostic errors. Paper 2 (Baltruschat) proves the solution paradigm works — AI worklist prioritization reduces turnaround by 56%. Paper 3 (Dippel) validates the exact technical approach — CTransPath plus anomaly detection at clinical-grade performance. Paper 4 (Chen) provides foundational scientific validation — pretrained pathology embeddings generalize across tissue types and tasks.

qa_pairs.question: What is CTransPath?
qa_pairs.answer: CTransPath is a computational pathology foundation model based on the Swin Transformer architecture (Swin-Tiny variant). It encodes histopathology image patches into 768-dimensional feature vectors that capture morphological patterns. PathoIntern uses CTransPath to generate embeddings for each blood smear patch, which are then used for anomaly detection and similarity search. The model uses a modified ConvStem patch embedding layer and requires timm version 0.5.4 specifically.

qa_pairs.question: Why doesn't PathoIntern use classification?
qa_pairs.answer: PathoIntern deliberately avoids classification because classification implies diagnosis. Instead, it uses embedding-based similarity and anomaly detection — measuring how far a patch deviates from normal patterns and which previously reviewed cases it resembles most. This approach is scientifically validated (Dippel et al., 2024) and keeps the system firmly in the non-diagnostic triage space. The previously identified research papers that used YOLO/CNN classification were rejected because they align with replacing pathologist judgment, not assisting it.

qa_pairs.question: What tech stack does PathoIntern use?
qa_pairs.answer: PathoIntern uses a three-tier architecture: (1) Frontend — Next.js 14 with App Router, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS, running on port 3000. (2) Backend — Python FastAPI with async SQLAlchemy 2.0, running on port 8000. (3) Database — PostgreSQL 15 with the pgvector extension for vector similarity search. The ML pipeline uses PyTorch with CTransPath (Swin-Tiny) for embedding generation, and timm 0.5.4 is pinned as a required dependency.

qa_pairs.question: How is the backend structured?
qa_pairs.answer: The FastAPI backend has 6 API routers: auth, patches, embeddings, scores, verdicts, and audit. It follows a service layer pattern with dedicated services for each domain: patch_service, embedding_service, scoring_service, verdict_service, audit_service, and data_loader. The ML pipeline includes the CTransPath encoder (ctranspath.py) and scoring algorithms (scoring.py) with AnomalyDetector, SimilaritySearcher, and CriticalityScorer classes.

qa_pairs.question: What database does PathoIntern use?
qa_pairs.answer: PathoIntern uses PostgreSQL 15 with the pgvector extension. The database has 6 tables: users, patches, embeddings, scores, verdicts, and audit_logs. The pgvector extension enables vector similarity search — storing 768-dimensional CTransPath embeddings and performing cosine distance queries to find similar patches. All database operations use async SQLAlchemy 2.0 with asyncpg as the driver.

qa_pairs.question: How does authentication work in PathoIntern?
qa_pairs.answer: PathoIntern uses JWT (JSON Web Token) authentication with HS256 signing. Passwords are hashed using bcrypt directly (not passlib, which is unmaintained). There are three roles: technologist, pathologist, and admin. Technologists can upload patches but cannot submit verdicts or access audit logs. Only pathologist and admin roles can submit verdicts. Admin users have additional access to user management and certain about pages. Login is rate-limited to 5 requests per minute per IP using slowapi.

qa_pairs.question: What is the audit trail?
qa_pairs.answer: The audit trail is an immutable, append-only log stored in the audit_logs table. Every action in the system — uploads, embedding generation, scoring, review, verdict submission — is recorded with full attribution (who, what, when). There are no DELETE or UPDATE endpoints for audit logs. This ensures complete traceability and accountability for every AI-assisted triage decision. The audit middleware also logs all API requests.

qa_pairs.question: How is PathoIntern deployed?
qa_pairs.answer: PathoIntern is deployed on a DigitalOcean droplet using Docker Compose. There are two environments: QA (qa.pathointern.ca) and Production (pathointern.ca). Nginx serves as a reverse proxy with TLS termination via Let's Encrypt certificates. CI/CD is handled by GitHub Actions — pushes to the develop branch auto-deploy to QA, pushes to main auto-deploy to production. Multi-stage Docker builds separate development and production targets.

qa_pairs.question: What is pgvector?
qa_pairs.answer: pgvector is a PostgreSQL extension that adds support for vector similarity search. In PathoIntern, each blood smear patch is encoded by CTransPath into a 768-dimensional vector (embedding). These embeddings are stored in a pgvector column, and the system uses cosine distance queries to find the top-k most similar patches in the reference corpus. This powers the 'Resemblance to Known Cases' panel in the review interface.

qa_pairs.question: How does the frontend communicate with the backend?
qa_pairs.answer: The frontend communicates via REST API calls with JWT Bearer token authentication. The API client is centralized in frontend/src/lib/api.ts, which provides typed fetch wrapper functions for all endpoints. Authentication state is managed through a React context (AuthContext.tsx). The frontend runs on Next.js 14 with App Router, and pages are organized under /phase1 (upload, results, review, audit) and /about sections.

qa_pairs.question: What are the brand colors of PathoIntern?
qa_pairs.answer: PathoIntern uses four brand colors: Navy (#1E3A5F) as the primary color for headers and text, Coral (#D64045) for alerts and emphasis, Teal (#2A9D8F) for positive indicators and success states, and Burnt Orange (#E76F51) for secondary accents. These colors are consistently applied across all pages using Tailwind CSS classes.

qa_pairs.question: How do I upload a blood smear image?
qa_pairs.answer: To upload a blood smear image: (1) Log in with your credentials. (2) Navigate to the Upload page under Phase 1. (3) Select one or more patch images (PNG or JPG format). (4) Click Upload. The system will save each image, generate a CTransPath embedding (768-dimensional vector), compute anomaly and criticality scores, and add the patch to the prioritized worklist. You can then review results on the Results page.

qa_pairs.question: What image formats does PathoIntern accept?
qa_pairs.answer: PathoIntern accepts PNG and JPG image formats for blood smear patch uploads. Images should be pre-extracted patches (cropped regions of a blood smear), not whole-slide images. Whole-slide image support (NDPI, SVS, TIFF formats) is planned for Phase 2.

qa_pairs.question: What happens after I upload an image?
qa_pairs.answer: After upload, the system performs three steps automatically: (1) Embedding generation — CTransPath encodes the image into a 768-dimensional L2-normalized vector and stores it in pgvector. (2) Anomaly scoring — the k-NN AnomalyDetector measures the embedding's distance from the normal-cell baseline. (3) Criticality scoring — the CriticalityScorer combines the anomaly score with similar-case context to produce a 0-100 criticality score and assigns a tier (Urgent, High, Elevated, or Routine). The patch then appears in the worklist.

qa_pairs.question: What is the Kaggle dataset used in PathoIntern?
qa_pairs.answer: PathoIntern's Phase 1 uses the Kaggle Parasite Dataset, which contains 34,298 blood smear patch images across 8 classes. These include normal morphology (RBCs, Leukocytes) and various parasite types. The dataset serves as the reference corpus — the normal images (10,371 RBC and Leukocyte patches) form the anomaly detection baseline, and the full labelled corpus powers the similarity search for the 'Resemblance to Known Cases' panel.

qa_pairs.question: How are embeddings generated?
qa_pairs.answer: Embeddings are generated using the CTransPath model, a Swin-Tiny vision transformer pretrained on computational pathology images. Each blood smear patch is passed through the model, producing a 768-dimensional feature vector. This vector is L2-normalized (converted to a unit vector) before being stored in the pgvector database. The normalization ensures that cosine distance can be computed as a simple dot product subtraction: d(a,b) = 1 - a·b.

qa_pairs.question: What is the anomaly baseline?
qa_pairs.answer: The anomaly baseline is a collection of embeddings from patches with normal morphology — specifically, patches labelled as RBCs (red blood cells) and Leukocytes. The current baseline is built from 10,371 normal patches from the Kaggle corpus. When a new patch is analyzed, the AnomalyDetector measures its k-NN distance (k=10) from this baseline. The further a patch's embedding is from the normal baseline, the higher its anomaly score — indicating it may contain unusual morphological patterns.

qa_pairs.question: How does the data ingestion pipeline work?
qa_pairs.answer: The data ingestion pipeline has four steps: (1) Ingest — the ingest_kaggle script downloads and imports images from the Kaggle dataset, creating patch records in the database. (2) Embed — the generate_embeddings script runs each image through CTransPath and stores the 768-dim vectors in pgvector. (3) Build Baseline — the build_baseline script extracts embeddings for normal patches (RBCs, Leukocytes) and saves them as the anomaly detection baseline (anomaly_baseline.npz). (4) Score — the score_all script computes anomaly and criticality scores for all patches.

qa_pairs.question: Can I process data on a local machine instead of the server?
qa_pairs.answer: Yes. The recommended approach for large-scale data processing is to use a local GPU machine. For example, the Kaggle corpus was processed using a local RTX 4060 GPU at 76.6 patches per second (7.5 minutes total), then shipped to the server via scp and pg_dump. This avoids multi-hour CPU processing on the server. The local GPU pipeline approach is the recommended pattern for future corpus updates.

qa_pairs.question: How does the scoring system work?
qa_pairs.answer: PathoIntern uses a three-component scoring system: (1) Anomaly Score — k-NN cosine distance from the normal-cell baseline, measuring how much a patch deviates from typical normal morphology. (2) Similarity Search — pgvector finds the top-5 most similar patches from the labelled reference corpus, providing visual context. (3) Criticality Score — a 0-100 composite score that combines anomaly distance with similar-case context, including boosts for close matches to known disease cases. The criticality score determines the triage tier.

qa_pairs.question: What are the triage tiers?
qa_pairs.answer: PathoIntern assigns patches to four triage tiers based on the criticality score: Urgent (score 80-100) — highest anomaly signal, should be reviewed first. High (score 60-79) — significant deviation from normal patterns. Elevated (score 40-59) — moderate anomaly signal. Routine (score 0-39) — closest to normal baseline patterns. The worklist is sorted by criticality score in descending order so the most anomalous cases appear first.

qa_pairs.question: What does the criticality score represent?
qa_pairs.answer: The criticality score is a 0-100 integer that represents how much a blood smear patch deviates from normal morphological patterns for triage prioritization purposes. It is NOT a diagnostic probability. A higher score means the patch's embedding is further from the normal baseline and may resemble known disease cases in the reference corpus. The score combines anomaly distance, similarity to disease cases, and close-match confidence boosts.

qa_pairs.question: How does anomaly detection work?
qa_pairs.answer: The AnomalyDetector uses k-NN (k-nearest neighbors with k=10) cosine distance to measure how far a patch's embedding is from the normal-morphology baseline. Because all embeddings are L2-normalized unit vectors, cosine distance is computed as d(a,b) = 1 - a·b. The 95th percentile of within-normal k-NN distances is used as a calibration reference, doubled to give headroom. A patch deviating by 2x the normal spread scores 1.0 (maximum anomaly).

qa_pairs.question: What is the similarity search?
qa_pairs.answer: The similarity search uses pgvector to find the top-5 most similar patches from the labelled Kaggle reference corpus. Only labelled patches are included in the reference pool — user-uploaded patches (which have no label) are excluded to prevent circular references. The similar patches are displayed in the 'Resemblance to Known Cases' panel with color-coded badges: teal for Normal (RBCs/Leukocyte), coral for Non-routine (disease classes), and grey for Unclassified.

qa_pairs.question: What does the worklist show?
qa_pairs.answer: The worklist displays all scored patches sorted by criticality score in descending order, so the most anomalous cases appear first. Each entry shows the patch image, criticality score, tier badge, and review status. The worklist supports filtering by tier (Urgent, High, Elevated, Routine) and review status (Pending, Reviewed). Pagination and counts are server-side for accuracy. Pathologists work through the list, reviewing cases and submitting verdicts.

qa_pairs.question: What is a verdict?
qa_pairs.answer: A verdict is a pathologist's clinical assessment of a scored patch. There are three verdict types: Agree (the pathologist concurs with the AI tier assignment), Disagree (the pathologist believes the tier is incorrect), and Modify (the pathologist adjusts the assessment). For Disagree and Modify verdicts, the pathologist must provide written notes explaining their reasoning. Each verdict includes a verdict score (0-100) — for Agree, it auto-populates from the criticality score. Only one verdict per patch is allowed, and only the original reviewer can update it.

qa_pairs.question: What are normal labels in the dataset?
qa_pairs.answer: In PathoIntern, the normal labels are RBCs (red blood cells) and Leukocyte. Patches with these labels represent normal blood cell morphology and form the anomaly detection baseline. Any other label (such as Plasmodium vivax, Plasmodium falciparum, etc.) represents a non-routine or disease morphology. Patches with no label (user uploads) are treated as unclassified and are excluded from the reference pool.

qa_pairs.question: How are the reference cases displayed?
qa_pairs.answer: Reference cases are displayed in the 'Resemblance to Known Cases' panel on the review page. The panel shows the top-5 most similar patches from the labelled corpus, with color-coded morphology badges: teal badges for Normal cases (RBCs, Leukocyte), coral badges for Non-routine cases (disease classes), and grey badges for Unclassified cases. The display order prioritizes non-normal cases first to give pathologists immediate context about potential disease patterns.

qa_pairs.question: What is the safety disclaimer?
qa_pairs.answer: Every results and review page in PathoIntern displays a non-dismissible safety disclaimer banner. This banner reminds users that PathoIntern is a non-diagnostic triage assistant and that all clinical decisions must be made by a licensed pathologist. The disclaimer cannot be closed or hidden — it is an architectural constraint, not a user preference. This ensures that no user can interact with AI-generated scores without being aware of the system's non-diagnostic nature.

qa_pairs.question: How do I get an account on PathoIntern?
qa_pairs.answer: To get an account on PathoIntern, you need to contact the system administrator. Currently, user registration is handled through the admin panel — an admin user creates your account with your username, password, and assigned role (pathologist, technologist, or admin). Self-registration is not available to maintain controlled access to the clinical triage system. Contact the project team to request access.

qa_pairs.question: What user roles exist in PathoIntern?
qa_pairs.answer: PathoIntern has three user roles: (1) Technologist — can upload patch images into the triage pipeline and view processing status, but cannot submit verdicts or access audit logs. This role is designed for lab staff who prepare and digitize slides. (2) Pathologist — can upload patches, view results, review the worklist, submit verdicts, and view the audit trail. This is the primary clinical user role. (3) Admin — has all pathologist permissions plus user management (creating and managing user accounts) and access to additional about pages (Personas, User Stories, Roadmap).

qa_pairs.question: Who can submit verdicts?
qa_pairs.answer: Only authenticated users with the pathologist or admin role can submit verdicts. Technologists cannot submit verdicts — they receive a 403 Forbidden response if they attempt to do so. This enforces the principle of pathologist authority — clinical assessment must come from a licensed professional. Each patch can have only one verdict, and only the original reviewer can update their verdict. For Disagree and Modify verdicts, the pathologist must provide written notes.

qa_pairs.question: How do I log in to PathoIntern?
qa_pairs.answer: Navigate to the login page at the root URL. Enter your username and password, then click Log In. The system uses JWT authentication — upon successful login, you receive an access token that is stored in your browser. Login is rate-limited to 5 attempts per minute per IP address for security. If you forget your password, contact the system administrator.

qa_pairs.question: How do I request admin access?
qa_pairs.answer: Admin access is granted by an existing admin user through the admin panel at /admin/users. If you need admin privileges, contact the project lead (Muthuraj Jayakumar) or any existing admin user. They can update your role from pathologist to admin through the user management interface. Admin access provides user management capabilities and access to additional project documentation pages.

qa_pairs.question: What are the password requirements?
qa_pairs.answer: Passwords must be at least 8 characters long. Usernames must be at least 3 characters and no more than 100 characters. Usernames are case-insensitive and are automatically converted to lowercase. Passwords are securely hashed using bcrypt before storage — they are never stored in plain text.
